title: Young Women Drive Alarming Surge in Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes
excerpt: A landmark Imperial College London study finds type 2 diabetes diagnoses among women in their twenties rose 69% over 13 years, with obesity at diagnosis climbing fastest in younger generations.
body:
• Type 2 diabetes diagnoses among women aged 20 to 29 in England surged 69% between 2011 and 2024, according to a first-of-its-kind population study published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe.
  • Younger adults are being diagnosed at significantly higher levels of obesity than previous generations, with BMI at diagnosis rising roughly twice as fast in under-40s compared to older adults.
  • The trend spans all ethnicities but is most pronounced among white, Asian and Black women aged 20 to 29, challenging assumptions that the crisis is confined to minority populations.
  • Researchers at Imperial College London are calling for a rethink of prevention strategies, including earlier use of GLP-1 medications and targeted weight-management support for younger adults.

Young women in England are driving a sharp rise in early-onset type 2 diabetes, a trend that researchers say demands an urgent overhaul of prevention strategies that have largely failed younger generations.

A new population-level study published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe found that diagnosis rates among adults under 40 are climbing rapidly, even as rates fall among those over 60. The sharpest increase was among women aged 20 to 29, whose age-standardized incidence rose 69% between 2011 and 2024. Men in the same age bracket saw a 43% increase.

A Generational Divide

The research, led by Imperial College London, analyzed data from the English National Diabetes Audit covering the entire population. It is the first study to break down new type 2 diabetes diagnoses nationally by age, sex and ethnicity simultaneously.

The findings reveal what researchers describe as a "clear generational divide." While older adults — who still account for the majority of diagnoses — are seeing incidence decline by roughly 2% per year among those aged 60 to 79, the trajectory for younger adults is heading in the opposite direction.

"We have known for a long time that obesity is linked to type 2 diabetes, but what is new from this study is the scale of the change occurring in younger adults."

— Dr. Shivani Misra, Imperial College London

Obesity at Diagnosis Is Getting Worse

The study also documented a striking shift in body weight at the time of diagnosis. Average BMI at diagnosis rose five to seven percent among under-40s during the study period, compared with two to three percent in those over 40. Among white women diagnosed at younger ages, average BMI at diagnosis approached 40 kg/m², a level classified as severe obesity.

Dr. Misra, a clinical associate professor in the Department of Metabolism, Digestion and Reproduction, said the earlier onset of severe obesity appears to be pulling down the age at which people develop diabetes, with serious long-term consequences including heart disease, kidney failure and poor pregnancy outcomes.

Not Just an Ethnic Minority Problem

Previous discussions of rising diabetes rates among younger adults have tended to focus on ethnic minority populations. While South Asian, Black and other minority groups remain disproportionately affected by early-onset type 2 diabetes, this analysis shows the increase is broadening well beyond those communities.

The rise was particularly noticeable among white, Asian and Black women aged 20 to 29, and among white women aged 30 to 39. Dr. Misra noted that this public health challenge is now broadening across an entire generation, regardless of ethnicity.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The findings carry particular relevance for South Asian communities worldwide. People of South Asian descent are already known to develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMI thresholds than white populations, and the disease tends to progress more aggressively. For Indian-origin families in the UK and beyond, the accelerating trend among younger women underscores the need for earlier screening and intervention, particularly for women of childbearing age.

The International Diabetes Federation has noted that globally, the incidence of type 2 diabetes among women aged 10 to 24 more than doubled between 1990 and 2021, with the growth rate of diabetes-related mortality among women nearly four times that of men.

Prevention Needs Rethinking

The authors say current approaches to diabetes prevention appear to be working less well in younger generations. They point to the widespread availability and marketing of unhealthy foods, increasingly sedentary lifestyles and what they call an "obesogenic environment" that young people seem particularly vulnerable to.

Potential strategies include earlier risk identification, encouraging diabetes prevention program participation at younger ages, earlier deployment of GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide, and intensive lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery for those with severe obesity.

"If we are serious about reducing the future burden of type 2 diabetes, we need stronger public health measures that create healthier environments and help prevent type 2 diabetes from developing in the first place."

— Dr. Shivani Misra, Imperial College London

What to Watch

Helen Kirrane, head of policy at Diabetes UK, called the findings "deeply concerning," noting that type 2 diabetes is more aggressive when diagnosed in younger people. The organization is pushing for government action including restrictions on unhealthy food promotion.

The researchers are also calling for age-stratified analyses to become routine in diabetes surveillance, warning that national averages may be masking critical shifts in specific population groups.
